pages.title: Kanade Architects
pages.content:
§ 01 — Graphic · Identity · 2026

An identity drawn on a 6 mm grid.

Client: Kanade Architects

Fig. 01 — Identity for Kanade Architects.

Brief

Kanade Architects had grown from two partners to fourteen people and still used a logo drawn in a weekend. They wanted something as calm and exact as their buildings, and a system junior staff could use without asking.

Approach

We drew the wordmark on the same 6 mm grid the practice uses for its working drawings, then built every piece of stationery, the drawing title block and the slide template on that grid. One weight of one typeface, one grey, one ochre dot for the founding date.

Outcome

The practice now produces its own competition boards in the new system. Print costs fell by a third because everything runs on two papers and one colour.

Credits

  • Art direction: Mio Arai
  • Type and grid: Mio Arai, Ren Okabe
  • Print: Tsukimi Printing Works (fictional)

pages.title: Mizuho Ceramics Fair
pages.content:
§ 02 — Advertising · Poster campaign · 2025

Three posters for a ceramics fair.

Client: Mizuho Ceramics Fair

Fig. 01 — Poster campaign for Mizuho Ceramics Fair.

Brief

A small regional ceramics fair needed one campaign to run on station boards, in shop windows and online, on a budget for three print runs.

Approach

Instead of photographing pots, we reduced each day of the fair to a mark: a glaze drop, a kiln line, a foot ring. One poster per day, the same grid, the same ochre.

Outcome

Visitors rose by 40 percent on the year before. Two of the posters are now sold at the fair itself.

Credits

  • Art direction: Ren Okabe
  • Design: Ren Okabe, Mio Arai
  • Copy: Saki Tanabe

Discipline Advertising

pages.title: Hoshino Tea Rooms
pages.content:
§ 03 — Advertising · Campaign · 2026

Quiet Hours, a campaign for slow afternoons.

Client: Hoshino Tea Rooms

Fig. 01 — Campaign for Hoshino Tea Rooms.

Brief

Hoshino Tea Rooms wanted weekday afternoons as busy as weekends, without discounting and without looking like a chain.

Approach

We wrote one line, “An hour with nothing in it”, and set it beside a large, almost empty composition. Street posters, a short film for the window screen and a printed card handed out at the counter.

Outcome

Weekday afternoon covers grew by a quarter across three rooms over the campaign’s twelve weeks.

Credits

  • Creative direction: Ren Okabe
  • Copy: Saki Tanabe
  • Photography: studio

pages.title: Tomoe Furniture
pages.content:
§ 04 — Web · Website · 2026

A website that loads like a showroom.

Client: Tomoe Furniture

Fig. 01 — Website for Tomoe Furniture.

Brief

Tomoe makes oak furniture to order. Their old site was a slow template full of carousels, and most visitors left before the first photograph loaded.

Approach

One long, quiet page per piece: a large photograph, the dimensions in a table, the wood, the price and the waiting time. No carousels, no pop-ups, system fonts in the shop, under 300 KB a page.

Outcome

Pages load in under a second on a phone. Enquiries per visit doubled in the first two months.

Credits

  • Design: Saki Tanabe
  • Build: Saki Tanabe
  • Photography: Tomoe workshop

Discipline Web

pages.title: Ishigaki Paper Mill
pages.content:
§ 05 — Graphic · Packaging · 2025

Packaging for a paper mill’s first shop.

Client: Ishigaki Paper Mill

Fig. 01 — Packaging for Ishigaki Paper Mill.

Brief

A family paper mill opened its first shop and needed boxes, bags and labels that showed off its own paper rather than covering it.

Approach

We left the boards bare. A single blind-debossed mark, a small label with the paper’s weight and fibre, and one ochre box for gifts.

Outcome

The packaging now doubles as the sample book: customers order the paper the box is made from.

Credits

  • Design: Mio Arai
  • Structure: Ren Okabe
  • Paper: Ishigaki Paper Mill

Discipline Graphic

pages.title: Shirokane Press
pages.content:
§ 06 — Web · Web and editorial · 2025

An online reader for a small publisher.

Client: Shirokane Press

Fig. 01 — Web and editorial for Shirokane Press.

Brief

Shirokane Press publishes four art books a year and wanted readers to browse each one online before ordering.

Approach

A page-turning reader built on plain HTML: spreads load one at a time, captions are real text, and the page grid of every book is reused for its web page.

Outcome

Pre-orders opened two weeks earlier than usual and the first run sold out before printing.

Credits

  • Design: Saki Tanabe, Mio Arai
  • Build: Saki Tanabe
  • Editorial: Shirokane Press

Discipline Web

Year 2025

posts.title: Why every identity starts with a grid
posts.excerpt: Before a single letter is drawn, we decide the spacing that everything else will share.
posts.content:
A grid is a promise that the small things will agree with each other: the logo, the margin of a letterhead, the gap above a caption.

For Kanade Architects we borrowed the 6 mm grid from their own drawings. The identity felt familiar to them on the first day, because it already was.

posts.title: Choosing paper for a short print run
posts.excerpt: Two papers, one weight each, and a printer who will tell you the truth.
posts.content:
Short runs make paper the most visible decision in the job. We keep to two stocks per identity: one smooth for text, one with a little tooth for covers and cards.

Ask the printer for a blank dummy before you sign anything off. It costs a day and saves the job.

posts.title: Three posters, not thirty
posts.excerpt: A small campaign is stronger when every piece has a reason to exist.
posts.content:
For the Mizuho Ceramics Fair we made one poster per day of the fair and nothing else. Each one had a single mark and the same line of type.

Fewer pieces meant better print, better placement and a campaign people remembered by its shapes.

posts.title: Writing a brief we can say yes to
posts.excerpt: Six questions that make the first call useful for both sides.
posts.content:
The best briefs we receive are under a page. They say who the work is for, why it is needed now, and what a good result would change.

A budget range, even a rough one, is the kindest thing a client can include. It lets us propose the right project instead of guessing.

posts.title: Fast, quiet websites
posts.excerpt: No carousels, no pop-ups and pages under 300 KB: the rules behind our websites.
posts.content:
A quiet website is mostly things left out. Every page we build starts from plain HTML and earns each script it loads.

The Tomoe Furniture site has one photograph per screen and a table of dimensions. It loads in under a second on a phone, and enquiries doubled.

posts.title: Alt text is part of the design
posts.excerpt: We write image descriptions in the layout file, next to the picture, not at the end.
posts.content:
Alt text written last is written badly. We draft it while choosing the photograph, when we still remember why it is there.

It is also the best test of an image: if we cannot say what it adds in one sentence, it probably does not belong on the page.
